title: The cell membrane, diffusion, osmosis and active transport
blurb: Explain how substances cross the cell membrane and predict what hypertonic, hypotonic and isotonic solutions do to cells.
question: A lab instructor drops red blood cells into three beakers: distilled water, 0.9% saline and a concentrated salt solution. What happens to the cells in each beaker, and which way does the water move?

teach.body: Formal definition: the cell (plasma) membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins, cholesterol (in animal cells) and glycoproteins, described by the fluid mosaic model; it is selectively permeable. Plain English: the membrane is a flexible, oily double layer dotted with protein doors. Small nonpolar molecules slip straight through, while ions and larger polar molecules need a protein door, and some cargo needs energy to get across.

teach.caption: Phagocytosis is "cell eating" (a neutrophil engulfing bacteria); pinocytosis is "cell drinking"; receptor-mediated endocytosis takes in LDL cholesterol.

teach.body: Osmosis is the movement of WATER across a selectively permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration (more water) to a region of higher solute concentration (less water). The solute stays put because it cannot cross; the water moves instead. Rate of any diffusion rises with a steeper concentration gradient, higher temperature, smaller molecules, greater surface area and shorter distance.

teach.h: Tonicity: the solution compared with the cell
teach.caption: 0.9% NaCl (normal saline) is isotonic to human cells, which is why it is used for IV fluids.

teach.caption: Active transport moves substances from LOW to HIGH concentration using carrier proteins (pumps) and ATP.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Carlos and the three beakers
teach.body: Carlos, a pre-nursing student, places red blood cells in three beakers. Distilled water has less solute than the cytoplasm (hypotonic), so water rushes in and the cells swell and burst: hemolysis. 0.9% saline is isotonic, so there is no net water movement and the cells keep their shape. Concentrated salt solution is hypertonic, so water leaves the cells and they shrink and crenate. In every case it is water, not salt, that moves.

teach.text: Three classic reversals: (1) osmosis is the movement of WATER, not solute; (2) water moves TOWARD the higher solute concentration; (3) HYPERtonic solutions shrink cells and HYPOtonic solutions swell them. Also: facilitated diffusion uses a protein but NO ATP.

items: Fluid mosaic model: phospholipid bilayer with proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins; selectively permeable.
Passive (no ATP, high to low): simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis.
Active (ATP): pumps against the gradient (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in), endocytosis, exocytosis.
Osmosis: water moves toward higher solute concentration.
Hypertonic: cell shrinks (crenation, plasmolysis). Hypotonic: cell swells (hemolysis; plant cells turgid). Isotonic: no net change.

summary: You can now describe the fluid mosaic membrane, sort transport into passive and active types, and explain the sodium-potassium pump. You can also predict whether a cell shrinks, swells or stays the same in a hypertonic, hypotonic or isotonic solution.

A.q: Which process moves glucose into a cell down its concentration gradient through a carrier protein without using ATP?
options: Simple diffusion
Active transport
Facilitated diffusion
Receptor-mediated endocytosis
A.why: Facilitated diffusion uses channel or carrier proteins (GLUT carriers for glucose) but no ATP, moving substances from high to low concentration.

whyNot.0: Simple diffusion passes straight through the bilayer with no protein; glucose is too large and polar for that.
whyNot.1: Active transport uses ATP and moves substances against their gradient.
whyNot.3: Receptor-mediated endocytosis uses ATP to bring in cargo such as LDL by vesicle.

A.q: A red blood cell is placed in a hypertonic solution. What happens to the cell?
options: Water leaves the cell and it crenates
Water enters the cell and it hemolyzes
Salt enters the cell and it swells
No net water moves and it keeps shape
A.why: A hypertonic solution has more solute than the cytoplasm, so water moves out by osmosis and the cell shrinks (crenation).

whyNot.1: Swelling and hemolysis happen in a hypotonic solution, not a hypertonic one.
whyNot.2: Osmosis moves water, not salt, and a hypertonic solution draws water out.
whyNot.3: No net water movement describes an isotonic solution.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the sodium-potassium pump?
options: Moves 3 K+ out and 2 Na+ in using ATP
Moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in without ATP
Moves Na+ and K+ down their gradients
Moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in using ATP
A.why: The Na+/K+ pump is active transport: it uses ATP to move 3 Na+ out of the cell and 2 K+ in, both against their gradients.

whyNot.0: The ions are reversed: sodium is pumped out and potassium is pumped in.
whyNot.1: Moving ions against their gradients requires ATP; this is active transport.
whyNot.2: The pump moves both ions against (up) their concentration gradients, not down them.

B.q: Two compartments are separated by a membrane permeable to water but not to glucose. Side X holds 5% glucose and side Y holds 10% glucose. What happens?
options: Water moves from X to Y
Water moves from Y to X
Glucose moves from Y to X
Neither water nor glucose moves
B.why: Water moves by osmosis toward the higher solute concentration, so it flows from side X (5%) to side Y (10%).

whyNot.1: This reverses osmosis: water moves toward the more concentrated side, which is Y.
whyNot.2: The membrane is impermeable to glucose, so glucose cannot cross.
whyNot.3: A concentration difference exists, so there is net movement of water.

B.q: A neutrophil surrounds a bacterium with its membrane and takes it in inside a vesicle. Which process is this?
options: Pinocytosis
Phagocytosis
Exocytosis
Facilitated diffusion
B.why: Phagocytosis ("cell eating") is endocytosis of large particles such as bacteria into a vesicle.

whyNot.0: Pinocytosis ("cell drinking") takes in fluid and dissolved solutes, not whole bacteria.
whyNot.2: Exocytosis moves material OUT of the cell by vesicle.
whyNot.3: Facilitated diffusion moves small molecules through membrane proteins, not whole cells.

B.q: Which change would INCREASE the rate at which oxygen diffuses across a membrane?
options: A thicker membrane to cross
A drop in the surrounding temperature
A smaller membrane surface area
A steeper concentration gradient
B.why: Diffusion is faster with a steeper concentration gradient, higher temperature, greater surface area and shorter distance.

whyNot.0: A thicker membrane increases the diffusion distance, slowing diffusion.
whyNot.1: Lower temperature slows molecular movement, so diffusion slows.
whyNot.2: Less surface area means fewer places to cross, so diffusion slows.

C.q: A patient receives an IV infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride. Compared with the patient's red blood cells, this solution is:
options: Hypotonic, so the cells swell
Isotonic, so no net water moves
Hypertonic, so the cells shrink
Hypotonic, so the cells shrink
C.why: 0.9% NaCl (normal saline) is isotonic to human cells, so there is no net movement of water and cells keep their size.

whyNot.0: Normal saline matches the solute concentration of the cells; it is not hypotonic.
whyNot.2: Normal saline is not more concentrated than the cytoplasm, so it does not shrink cells.
whyNot.3: This is wrong twice: normal saline is isotonic, and a hypotonic solution would make cells swell, not shrink.

C.q: A wilted lettuce leaf is placed in pure water and becomes crisp. Which explanation is correct?
options: Cells lose water and undergo plasmolysis
Cells take in water until they burst
Cells take in water and become turgid
Cells take in salt and become turgid
C.why: Pure water is hypotonic, so water enters the plant cells by osmosis; the cell wall stops them bursting and they become turgid.

whyNot.0: Plasmolysis happens in a hypertonic solution, where cells lose water and wilt further.
whyNot.1: The rigid cellulose cell wall prevents plant cells from bursting.
whyNot.3: Pure water contains no salt, and osmosis is the movement of water, not solute.

C.q: Which of these transport events requires ATP?
options: O2 diffusing straight across the lipid bilayer
Glucose entering through a GLUT carrier
Water crossing through aquaporin channels
Ca2+ pumped up its concentration gradient
C.why: Pumping an ion from low to high concentration is active transport, which uses ATP.

whyNot.0: Oxygen moves by simple diffusion, a passive process.
whyNot.1: Glucose moving down its gradient via GLUT is facilitated diffusion, which uses no ATP.
whyNot.2: Water through aquaporins is osmosis, a passive process.

reteach.title: Doors, turnstiles and elevators
reteach.question: Picture a crowded concert hall with a quiet street outside. How do people move between them, and when does it cost anything?

blocks.h: Moving with or against the crowd
blocks.body: People naturally spill from the packed hall to the empty street: that is diffusion, and it is free. Small, slim people squeeze through gaps in the wall (simple diffusion). Others need a specific door (facilitated diffusion), still free because they are moving with the crowd. Getting people back INTO the packed hall against the flow needs a paid elevator (active transport, ATP). Moving a whole group at once in a bus is bulk transport (endocytosis in, exocytosis out).

blocks.text: A door (protein) does not mean payment: facilitated diffusion uses a protein but no ATP. Only movement AGAINST the gradient, or by vesicle, costs ATP.

explain.body: A phospholipid bilayer: hydrophilic heads face the water on each side, hydrophobic tails face inward. Proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins sit in it like tiles in a mosaic, and the whole thing is fluid. It is selectively permeable and handles cell recognition and signaling.

test.q: The cell membrane is described by the "fluid mosaic" model because it is:
options: A rigid wall of cellulose and embedded proteins
A flexible bilayer studded with proteins
A single layer of fatty acid tails
A mesh of protein fibers holding water
test.why: The membrane is a fluid phospholipid bilayer with a mosaic of proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins embedded in it.

whyNot.0: Cellulose forms the plant cell wall, which is outside the membrane and not fluid.
whyNot.2: The membrane is a double layer (bilayer) of phospholipids, not a single layer.
whyNot.3: A mesh of protein fibers describes the cytoskeleton, not the membrane.

explain.body: No ATP; substances move from high to low concentration. Simple diffusion: small nonpolar molecules (O2, CO2) cross the bilayer directly. Facilitated diffusion: channels or carriers for glucose and ions. Osmosis: water, often through aquaporins.

test.q: Which substance crosses the membrane by simple diffusion directly through the phospholipid bilayer?
options: Carbon dioxide
Glucose
Sodium ions
Insulin protein
test.why: CO2 is small and nonpolar, so it diffuses straight through the lipid bilayer.

whyNot.1: Glucose is large and polar, so it needs GLUT carrier proteins (facilitated diffusion).
whyNot.2: Charged ions cannot cross the hydrophobic core; they need channels or pumps.
whyNot.3: Insulin is a large protein released by exocytosis, not by diffusion.

explain.body: Active transport uses ATP to move substances from low to high concentration through pumps: the Na+/K+ pump sends 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in. Bulk transport also uses ATP: endocytosis brings material in by vesicle, exocytosis releases it.

test.q: A neuron releases neurotransmitter by fusing vesicles with its plasma membrane. Which process is this?
options: Endocytosis
Pinocytosis
Exocytosis
Osmosis
test.why: Exocytosis releases the contents of vesicles out of the cell, as in neurotransmitter and hormone secretion.

whyNot.0: Endocytosis brings material INTO the cell.
whyNot.1: Pinocytosis is a type of endocytosis that takes in fluid.
whyNot.3: Osmosis is the passive movement of water, not vesicle release.

explain.body: Compare the solution with the cell. Hypertonic (more solute outside): water leaves, cell shrinks. Hypotonic (less solute outside): water enters, cell swells and may burst. Isotonic (0.9% NaCl for human cells): no net movement.

test.q: Red blood cells placed in distilled water swell and burst. Relative to the cells, the water was:
options: Hypotonic; water moved into the cells
Hypertonic; water moved into the cells
Hypertonic; salt moved out of the cells
Isotonic; water moved into the cells
test.why: Distilled water has less solute than the cytoplasm, so it is hypotonic; water floods in by osmosis and the cells hemolyze.

whyNot.1: A hypertonic solution would draw water OUT and shrink the cells.
whyNot.2: Distilled water is not hypertonic, and osmosis moves water, not salt.
whyNot.3: An isotonic solution causes no net water movement, so cells would not burst.
